::: {#exr-panda-draw-shirt}
The US government debt (usually called the "National Debt") is approximately $40 trillion as of early 2026. Written out, that's $40,000,000,000,000. Or, $4e13.

The "gross domestic product" (GDP) of the US is about $30 trillion per year. The per-year is important. It's the same quantity as $2.5 trillion per month, or $1 million per second, or $3000 trillion per century. 

Economic journalists often describe the debt condition of a country as ratio of debt to GDP. For instance, looking at the amounts $40 and $30 trillion, they would measure the US debt is 125% of GDP. A journalist's rule of thumb is that ratios above 100% are a sign of trouble.

1. What is the dimension of the quantity Debt/GDP?

```{mcq}
#| label: pds-1-dimension
#| inline: true
1. Dimensionless 
2. Time [correct]
3. Money^-1^
4. Time^-1^
```


Comparing GDP (dimension W T^-1^) with government debt (dimension W) makes sense only if we are interested in extracting the T component. The journalists' ratio of "125%" should really be stated as 1.25 years.

It is unclear what fundamental justification there is for treating a ratio of 1 year as the threshold for concern. Among other things, there are many other forms of debt: state and local government debt ($4 trillion in 2026), corporate debt ($16 trillion in 2026), and consumer debt ($18 trillion in 2026), which are not captured in the national debt figure. Add to this about $5 trillion in unfunded liabilities for state and local public pensions, $8 trillion for Federal civil and military pensions, and $25 trillion in the net present value of unfunded Social Security benefits. These figures total $76 trillion, about double the so-called "national debt."

More fundamentally, the Dept/GDP ratio says little about how expensive the debt is, that is, how much it costs to service the debt each year. `r xf("fig-pds-23s")` shows a fairly stable pattern of Dept/GDP over the last 15 years (excluding the 2020 spike in the COVID-19 pandemic). But the interest-expense/GDP ratio shows substantial changes over the last five years.

```{r}
#| label: fig-pds-23s
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "US National Debt to GDP Ratio with Interest Expense (2010-2026). [Data source](https://fiscaldata.treasury.gov/americas-finance-guide/national-debt/)"
library(ggplot2)
USstats <- readr::read_csv("../www/US_Debt_2010_2026.csv")
ggplot(USstats, aes(x = FY, y = Debt/GDP)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_line(aes(y = 20*InterestExpense/GDP), color="blue") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14 ) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits=c(0,2), sec.axis = sec_axis(~./20, name = "Interest Expense/GDP")) +
  geom_text(aes(label = "Interest Expense", y = 0.6, x = 2015), color = "blue") +
  geom_text(aes(label = "National Debt", y = 1.5, x = 2015)) +
  labs(x = "Year", y = "Debt/GDP")
```

:::
